source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty
finding: Plain entropy over answer strings mixes up wording and meaning. Semantic entropy groups sampled answers by mutual entailment, then takes entropy over meaning clusters. It predicts answer correctness better than sequence entropy, length-normalised entropy, lexical similarity and p(True).
numbers: Fig 1a: best AUROC on TriviaQA with OPT-30B (about 0.8), above all baselines; the gap grows with model size (2.7B to 30B). Open-book CoQA and closed-book TriviaQA.
limits: Tested on OPT up to 30B, QA only; entailment clustering needs a separate NLI model.
agent_relevance: S7 probe choice: sample several attempts, cluster by meaning, use cluster entropy as the uncertainty signal.

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty
finding: Counting the number of semantically distinct answers is already a usable uncertainty score, but entropy over the clusters is better.
numbers: Table 2: distinct answers 1.27 (correct) vs 1.77 (incorrect) on CoQA; 1.89 vs 3.89 on TriviaQA. AUROC semantic entropy 0.77 vs count 0.66 (CoQA); 0.83 vs 0.79 (TriviaQA).
limits: Count ignores how probability mass is spread across clusters.
agent_relevance: Cheap proxy: the number of distinct candidate answers in the S4 harvest is itself a signal; cluster sizes add more.

source: Kuhn, Gal, Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty
finding: Boundary condition: semantic entropy does not always win. At high sampling temperature, normalised entropy did better on CoQA and TriviaQA variants, and the best temperature trades answer accuracy against answer diversity.
numbers: Appendix temperature sweeps; accuracy of sampled answers fell to about 61% at a hot setting vs over 92% at lower ones. Authors say far fewer samples than prior work suffice.
limits: Result depends on temperature and sample count; one setting does not fit all.
agent_relevance: Use moderate-temperature draws for entropy estimates; do not use very hot draws.

source: Farquhar et al. (2024) Detecting hallucinations in LLMs using semantic entropy, Nature
finding: Nature version: semantic entropy detects confabulations (arbitrary wrong answers) across tasks without task data, and extends to paragraph generations by splitting into factual claims.
numbers: Averaged over 30 task-model combinations: semantic entropy AUROC 0.790; naive entropy 0.691; P(True) 0.698; embedding regression 0.687. Stable 0.78-0.81 across LLaMA 2, Falcon, Mistral, 7B to 70B. Datasets: TriviaQA, SQuAD, BioASQ, NQ-Open, SVAMP; FactualBio (GPT-4, 21 people, 150 claims).
limits: Catches confabulation (random errors) only, not consistent wrong answers from bad training data; costs 5-10 extra samples.
agent_relevance: Entropy of meaning is a stronger uncertainty gate than token entropy; gate extra effort on high semantic entropy (G12).

source: Farquhar et al. (2024) Detecting hallucinations in LLMs using semantic entropy, Nature
finding: Semantic entropy can drive refusal: the AURAC metric (accuracy after dropping the highest-entropy questions) improves over baselines.
numbers: AURAC = area under the rejection-accuracy curve; semantic entropy beats naive entropy and P(True) on it over five datasets.
limits: Exact AURAC values are in the figure, not recorded here.
agent_relevance: An abstain or escalate rule keyed on semantic entropy fits S8 verify and S9 look back.

source: Kossen et al. (2024) Semantic Entropy Probes: Robust and Cheap Hallucination Detection in LLMs
finding: A linear probe on the hidden state of one generation can predict semantic entropy, removing the 5-to-10-fold sampling cost. Probes trained on SE labels (no accuracy labels) generalise to new tasks better than probes trained on accuracy.
numbers: Table 1 in-distribution, SEP minus accuracy-probe AUROC: Mistral-7B +2.8 (se 1.4), Phi-3 +2.1, Llama-2-7B -0.5, Llama-2-70B +1.3; long-form Llama-2-70B -1.9, Llama-3-70B -2.0. Leave-one-task-out: SEPs consistently better, large gain on BioASQ.
quote: SEPs may be the best unsupervised method for hallucination detection
limits: Needs hidden-state access; not usable on closed API models.
agent_relevance: For an open-weights agent, entropy can be read from one pass; for API agents it must be sampled.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false when the format is right. Models can be trained to predict P(IK), the chance they know the answer; it partly generalises across tasks but is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: 52B Anthropic model; P(True) and P(IK) tested in and out of distribution; a 'None of the above' option harms calibration; RLHF miscalibration fixable by temperature tuning.
quote: Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks
limits: Calibration degrades after RLHF and on new tasks; proprietary model.
agent_relevance: Model confidence is usable but needs a held-out check, in line with G10.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022); Kuhn et al. (2023)
finding: P(True) is the self-evaluation baseline later entropy methods are compared to. Kuhn et al. reimplemented it at 10-shot on OPT-30B and it did dramatically worse than semantic entropy.
numbers: Original: 20-shot, 52B model. Kuhn: 10-shot, up to 30B.
limits: Reimplementation is smaller with fewer shots, so part of the gap reflects scale.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on asking the model whether its answer is true as the uncertainty signal.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT simulates future question-answer branches, scores each question by expected information gain (entropy reduction over a candidate set) and picks the best. It beats direct prompting and tree or reflection baselines on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Average success-rate gain of 38.1% over direct prompting across five datasets and several LLMs. GPT-4: DX 97.0% (vs 89.4% direct); MedDG 87.9% vs 74.9%; FloDial 67.8% vs 42.5%; 20Q Common 70.9% vs 49.0%, Thing 36.8% vs 30.8%. t-tests p<0.05.
limits: Cleanest with a closed candidate set; open-set version is weaker; noisy answers (no fever is not full exclusion) only handled approximately.
agent_relevance: Direct match for S7: pick the discriminating probe that splits remaining candidates most evenly.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: UoT also beats stronger reasoning wrappers, and plain CoT hurt on information seeking.
numbers: UoT beats CoT-SC by 33.8% and Reflexion by 29.9% on average; Original ToT by 28.3%, Adapted ToT by 12.4%; pruned UoT beats Adapted-ToT by 7.36%. On 20Q, CoT and PP with GPT-4 were worse than GPT-4 alone. Troubleshooting 43.7% to 67.3%.
limits: Averages over the paper's own datasets; no outside replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Explicit entropy scoring is what helped, not more reasoning text.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts
finding: Gains hold for a weaker open model and are larger where the plain model is weakest (difficulty boundary).
numbers: Llama 3 success: Common 47.7 to 56.5; Thing 14.8 to 24.8; DX 80.1 to 90.1; FloDial 29.9 to 46.4.
limits: Smaller gain on DX where the base is already high.
agent_relevance: Skip the entropy probe when the plain pass rate is already high (direct class).

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions: Preference Optimization and Expected Information Gain
finding: Open-source LLMs ask poor 20-questions questions as measured by EIG. Sampling several questions, scoring each by EIG, and training with DPO on high versus low EIG pairs makes Llama-2-Chat 7B ask better and win more.
numbers: Table (success rate, turns, EIG): INLG zero-shot 56.7%, 7.1, 0.34; fine-tuned 46.6%, 4.6, 0.41; DPO 68.9%, 5.2, 0.45. Things: zero-shot 51.1%, 7.5, 0.29; DPO 61.1%, 5.2, 0.40. Celebrities: zero-shot 71.1%, 7.6, 0.35; DPO 72.2%, 5.1, 0.47.
limits: 7B model, polar questions in a closed candidate set; plain fine-tuning lowered success in two sets (46.6% and 42.2%). Column labels read from a garbled table.
agent_relevance: EIG is a trainable and testable target; at inference one can sample k questions and pick the highest EIG with no training.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024)
finding: Models do better on concrete than abstract targets.
numbers: Concrete targets: 25.0% zero-shot, 37.5% DPO. Abstract: 7.7% zero-shot, 23.1% DPO.
limits: Small hand-checked sets.
agent_relevance: Expect more wasted probes when the hypothesis space is abstract; check the split before running a probe.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships: Asking Questions in Battleship with Language-Informed Program Sampling
finding: Language-informed program sampling: LLM proposes questions, they are translated to code, and each is scored by EIG. Best-of-k sampling reaches human mean information with small k.
numbers: Human data N=40, 605 question-board pairs, 18 boards: mean human EIG 1.27, best human 3.61; 97% of human questions had EIG>0. Single LLM samples (k=1) averaged EIG 0.65-0.66 for CodeLlama and GPT-4; at k=5 both approach the human mean.
limits: Even large k falls short of the top 10-20% of human questions.
agent_relevance: Sample-and-score by EIG is cheap and works; the score must be computed by code.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships
finding: LLMs fail to ground questions in the board state. GPT-4V did not improve with a visual or text-grid board over no board; few-shot examples helped everywhere.
numbers: Table 1 (k=1): GPT-4 EIG 0.65 to 0.77 across few-shot, zero-shot, no-board conditions; valid-program rate 0.40 to 0.88; informative rate 0.35 to 0.59 across rows.
limits: Early 2024 models.
agent_relevance: LLMs alone do not compute information gain over a state; code must evaluate it.

source: Grand et al. (2024) Loose LIPS Sink Ships
finding: Programs make EIG computable: the question becomes code run over sampled hypotheses (boards), giving exact expected entropy reduction.
numbers: Best question reached EIG 3.61 vs human mean 1.27.
limits: Needs a world model that can be sampled.
agent_relevance: Our discriminating test in S7 can be scored by running candidate programs on candidate inputs.

source: Handa et al. (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN uses Bayesian optimal experimental design to choose which question to ask and an LM only to word it. In user studies it elicits human preferences faster than LM-only questioning.
numbers: Metric: time-integrated delta accuracy (TIDA). OPEN pairwise questions beat LM-only pairwise questions. LM open-ended questions did well under LM prediction, but OPEN's own predictor gave the larger benefit.
limits: Exact TIDA numbers are in a figure and were not read.
agent_relevance: Split the job: code does the entropy scoring, the model does the wording.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Choosing clarifying questions by EIG over the space of solutions beats reasoning only in question space. Tested on code generation (HumanEval, APPS) after eliciting 4 requirements.
numbers: EIG-based strategies gave higher solution accuracy with fewer test cases queried; open questions beat binary ones; the gap shrinks for stronger models. GPT-4o-mini zero-shot on APPS is 35% vs 70% on the other benchmark.
quote: Shifts the load from implicit to explicit reasoning about the space of viable solutions
limits: Exact tables in appendix not read; 4-question budget only.
agent_relevance: Strong models gain less from explicit EIG: apply it where the plain model is unsure (G12).

source: Ton et al. (2024) Understanding Chain-of-Thought in LLMs: an Information-Theoretic Perspective
finding: Defines information gain per reasoning step as the change in log-probability of the correct final answer. Correct steps give positive gain, wrong steps low or negative gain. No step labels needed.
numbers: Toy arithmetic detection scores: IG 0.96, 0.98, 0.06 vs outcome reward model 0.77, 0.98, 0.54 (columns by condition). Also GSM8K and PRM800k.
limits: Needs the true answer to compute, so it is an evaluation tool, not a live signal.
agent_relevance: Per-step information gain could be a progress meter for S4 and S6 if a held-out answer proxy exists.

source: Delétang et al. (2023) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: A language model plus arithmetic coding is a lossless compressor, so prediction and compression are the same. Text-trained models compress other data better than special-purpose tools.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% and LibriSpeech to 16.4% of raw size; PNG 58.5%, FLAC 30.3%.
limits: Adjusted rates that count model parameters make big models worse than gzip on small data.
agent_relevance: Supports the MDL framing: shorter code counts only if model cost is counted.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly
finding: Across LLMs, bits per character on external text correlates almost linearly with average benchmark score.
numbers: Pearson -0.93, RMSE 3.1% on the average over knowledge, commonsense and coding. Single benchmarks: HellaSwag -0.881, TriviaQA -0.951, MMLU -0.890.
limits: Base models only; contamination screened with Min-K%; correlation, not cause.
agent_relevance: Compression loss is a label-free quality proxy for a model, not for a single answer.

source: Cui et al. (2025) The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models
finding: In RL for reasoning, policy entropy collapses early and performance saturates. Fitted law R = -a exp(H) + b: performance is bought with entropy. Entropy change is driven by the covariance of action probability and advantage.
numbers: Over 95% of entropy drop and performance gain happen early in training. Clip-Cov and KL-Cov kept entropy up; Qwen2.5-32B gains of 15.0% (AIME24) and 14.6% (AIME25) over GRPO.
limits: Training-time result on open Qwen-family models.
agent_relevance: Warns that sharpened distributions lose exploration; resampling at S3 needs real diversity.

source: Synthesis across Grand 2024, Mazzaccara 2024, Kobalczyk 2025
finding: Unaided LLM questions have low or zero expected information gain; sampling many and picking by EIG, or training on EIG, fixes much of it.
numbers: Grand k=1 EIG about 0.65 vs human 1.27, near human at k=5. Mazzaccara EIG 0.34 to 0.45 after DPO. Kobalczyk: EIG selection beat question-space reasoning.
limits: Different games, models and metrics; no common benchmark.
agent_relevance: Implement S7 probe choice as sample k, then score by code.

source: Synthesis of Kuhn 2023 and Farquhar 2024
finding: The semantic-entropy result grew from OPT-30B on two datasets (2023) to 30 task-model combinations and GPT-4 biographies (2024), with a lead over naive entropy of about 0.10 AUROC.
numbers: 0.790 vs 0.691 (Farquhar); Kuhn TriviaQA 0.83 vs lower baselines.
limits: Same lead group; independent use seen only in Kossen et al., who used it as a label.
agent_relevance: Moderate confidence the effect is real for factual QA.

source: Limits across studies (synthesis)
finding: Entropy signals miss consistent wrong answers, need many samples, and have mostly been tested on factual QA, not on multi-step reasoning or ARC-like puzzles.
numbers: Farquhar: detects only confabulation. Kuhn: temperature-dependent. UoT: closed candidate sets.
limits: No study found this session testing semantic entropy as a selector on puzzle tasks.
agent_relevance: Open gap: test cluster-entropy gating on our own benchmark before adopting it in S7.

source: Inference from Kuhn 2023 and self-consistency voting (synthesis)
finding: Semantic entropy as a gate has the same shape as majority voting: sample, group by meaning, look at the largest cluster. Entropy keeps the spread; the vote discards it.
numbers: Kuhn: AUROC 0.77-0.83 from cluster counts and entropy.
limits: Structural inference, not a measured comparison against majority vote.
agent_relevance: Use cluster spread as a signal of when to spend more attempts.
